planting.note: Direct-sow on bare, well-drained soil in early spring or fall; seeds need light and should barely be covered.

directions: Sow seed directly on disturbed, lean soil in spring or autumn and press lightly into the surface, since seedlings establish best with light exposure and poor to average fertility. This wiry, rhizome-spreading perennial produces narrow blue-green foliage and tall racemes of small two-toned yellow-and-orange snapdragon-like flowers from midsummer into fall. It spreads aggressively by both creeping roots and self-sown seed, so site it in meadow plantings, roadside strips, or naturalized areas rather than tidy borders unless root barriers are used. Established clumps need no supplemental feeding and tolerate drought, poor soil, and neglect once settled.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow on gritty, sharply drained scree or raised-bed mix; a period of cold is beneficial for even germination.

directions: Sow onto gritty, mineral scree or a raised rock-garden bed where winter wet drains away instantly, since this high-alpine species is short-lived in heavy or waterlogged soil. It forms low, trailing mats of glaucous blue-gray foliage studded with small two-toned violet-purple and orange flowers through summer. Best treated as a true scree or trough plant, tucked between stones where its roots stay cool and dry; top-dress annually with fine grit to keep the crown from rotting. Short-lived even in ideal conditions, but self-sows lightly onto open gravel to replace itself.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery pots in fall or early spring in cool, moisture-retentive soil; handle with gloves, as all plant parts are toxic.

directions: Plant divisions in cool, humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged, in a site with morning sun and afternoon shade in warmer climates. This compact selection of Chinese monkshood bred by Georg Arends forms sturdy, self-supporting clumps of deeply lobed dark foliage topped by dense branching spikes of violet-blue hooded flowers in late summer into fall, later than most other monkshoods. Mulch roots to keep them cool and divide only when clumps become congested, since plants resent frequent disturbance. Wear gloves when handling any part of the plant, as the roots, foliage, and flowers contain potent alkaloids.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall for first-year rosettes and second-year bloom, or very early spring; prefers lean, well-drained, alkaline soil.

directions: Direct-sow on lean, sharply drained, preferably chalky or alkaline soil in fall, letting seedlings overwinter as low bristly rosettes before sending up flowering stems the following summer. Slender upright spikes carry a long succession of narrow, deep crimson-red tubular flowers that are irresistible to bumblebees and other long-tongued pollinators, blooming over many weeks in midsummer. Being a biennial or short-lived perennial, it performs best when a few plants are allowed to self-seed each year to maintain a continuous stand. Avoid rich, damp soils and heavy mulch, which encourage rot and floppy, overfed growth.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes, as plants are slow to establish from direct seed.

directions: Start seed indoors under light since germination is slow and uneven, then transplant seedlings into well-drained garden soil once frost danger has passed, taking care not to disturb the brittle taproot. This dwarf, compact selection from the Astra breeding series stays neat and ground-hugging, bearing inflated balloon-shaped buds that pop open into star-shaped soft pink flowers over a long summer season. Its tidy habit makes it well suited to container culture, rock gardens, and the front of mixed borders where taller balloon flowers would flop. Plants emerge late in spring, so mark their location to avoid accidental digging before new growth appears.

planting.note: Plant divisions or young plants in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil; spreads by rhizomes so allow room or confine with edging.

directions: Plant divisions in ordinary, well-drained garden soil in sun to light shade, where the spreading rhizomes will knit together into a billowing clump within a season or two. This old cottage-garden heirloom carries clustered, fully double pink flowers with a soft clove-like fragrance over upright stems from early to midsummer, lacking the viable seed of the wild single-flowered species since the doubled blooms are sterile. Because it spreads steadily underground, it suits informal borders, cottage gardens, and naturalized areas but benefits from an edging barrier in small formal beds. Cut plants back hard after the main bloom flush to tidy foliage and occasionally prompt a lighter rebloom.
